title: The Devout Israelite

full_text:
In an ancient city lived a poor weaver who was celebrated among his neighbors for his profound piety, contentment, and unwavering trust in divine providence. Though he laboured at his loom from dawn until dusk, he earned barely enough to purchase a small measure of barley meal for his wife and himself each day.

A severe famine struck the land. Grain prices soared, the mills stopped, and the streets were filled with starving people. The weaver and his wife had only a single small loaf of barley bread remaining in their clay jar, which they intended to share for their evening supper.

As they sat down to break the bread, a feeble knock was heard at the door. An elderly stranger, shivering with cold and leaning upon a staff, stood upon the threshold, saying: 'O people of the house! I have not tasted food for three days, and my soul is fainting within me. Give me a morsel, for the sake of the Merciful Creator!'

The weaver's wife looked at the single loaf, and then at her husband. The weaver smiled with radiant serenity, took the loaf, divided it in two, and placed the larger half in the beggar’s trembling hands.

The beggar ate with tears of relief, blessed the household with ancient words of abundance, and departed.

The weaver and his wife sat down to share the remaining crust, their hearts filled with peaceful contentment. When the wife went to wipe the crumbs from the clay flour-jar, she gasped in astonishment: the jar, which had been empty for weeks, was brimming over with finest white wheat flour!

Day after day, as long as the famine lasted, the jar never emptied. The weaver baked bread each morning, distributing loaves to all the starving families in his street without charging a single copper, proving that the hand that gives in the hour of need will never be empty of blessings.
moral: Sharing one's last bread in selfless charity multiplies blessings and banishes hunger forever.
